tEn: Designing the Future: Brian Lovin on AI, Notion, and Blurring Roles
tZh: 设计未来：Brian Lovin 谈 AI、Notion 与角色融合
sEn: Brian Lovin shares how designers must embrace adaptability and AI, drawing from his intense onboarding at Notion and work on AI agents.
sZh: Brian Lovin 分享了设计师如何拥抱适应性与 AI，结合他在 Notion 的紧张入职经历和 AI 代理工作。

consensus.en: Designers should prototype in code and design the harness for agents, not just Figma.
consensus.zh: 设计师应该在代码中做原型并设计智能体的“缰绳”，而不只是用 Figma。

consensus.en: Design, PM, and engineering boundaries are blurring; focus on shipping great software, not titles.
consensus.zh: 设计、产品管理和工程的边界正在模糊；专注于交付优质软件，而不是头衔。

consensus.en: AI harnesses change every six months; stay adaptable and understand why.
consensus.zh: AI 的“缰绳”每六个月就会变一次；保持适应并理解背后的原因。

consensus.en: High-quality prompts and technical vocabulary significantly improve AI output.
consensus.zh: 高质量的提示词和技术词汇能显著提升 AI 的输出效果。

consensus.en: AI is not magic; understanding underlying computer systems makes you more effective.
consensus.zh: AI 不是魔法；理解底层计算机系统能让你更高效。

consensus.en: The ability to focus without distraction is a competitive advantage in the chaotic AI era.
consensus.zh: 在混乱的 AI 时代，不被干扰的专注能力是一种竞争优势。

contrarian.en: Despite AI hype, models are still bad at final visual polish; hand-editing code is necessary.
contrarian.zh: 尽管 AI 被大肆炒作，模型在最终视觉打磨上仍然糟糕；手工编辑代码是必要的。

contrarian.en: The “nobody writes code” meta is false; reading and writing code still ensures quality.
contrarian.zh: 「没人写代码」的说法是假的；阅读和编写代码仍是质量的保证。

contrarian.en: Self-reported AI productivity gains may be illusory; more output but lower quality and more fixes.
contrarian.zh: 自我报告的 AI 生产力提升可能是虚幻的；产出更多但质量更低、修复更多。

contrarian.en: Expect an AI burnout and come-down soon; unsustainable intensity leads to hitting a wall.
contrarian.zh: 预计 AI 倦怠和回落即将到来；不可持续的高强度会导致撞墙。

contrarian.en: Knowing how to code gives a major advantage with AI because you know the right vocabulary.
contrarian.zh: 会编程能让你在用 AI 时获得巨大优势，因为你知道正确的词汇。

contrarian.en: Companies that don't reposition for an AI-legible ecosystem risk becoming obsolete.
contrarian.zh: 不针对 AI 可读生态系统进行重新定位的公司，有被淘汰的风险。

turns.en: I've found a little bit of inner peace with the fact that it's just going to keep changing. My job is to understand what's happening and why it's happening — why is it good at writing code, and what are the implications of that? Okay, well, it needs a safe space to execute that code. Then you look around and everyone's spinning up sandboxes. Sandboxes are slow, so let's make them faster. All these things are downstream consequences of the agent harness changing. It's changed every six months for the last couple of years, and I assume that will continue.
turns.zh: 我已经找到了一点内心的平静，接受这件事会不断变化这个事实。我的工作是理解正在发生什么、为什么发生——为什么它擅长写代码，这又意味着什么？好，那它需要一个安全的环境来执行代码。然后你环顾四周，大家都在建沙盒。沙盒很慢，那我们就让它更快。所有这些都是智能体框架变化的后续结果。过去几年里，它每六个月就变一次，我觉得这种变化会继续下去。

turns.en: Clarifying question about the prototyping playground you built. I've seen a bit of it, but help me understand where it sits on the spectrum. On one end, it's a fresh, throwaway build with no context. On the other end, it's a near-perfect copy of the codebase that you've kept reasonably up to date. Where does it fall? I don't often see that level of fidelity. My guess is somewhere in the middle. Tell me a bit about that.
turns.zh: 关于你搭建的原型游乐场，我想澄清一下。我见过一点，但帮我弄清楚它处在这个光谱的哪个位置。一端是全新的、随便搭的、没有上下文的构建；另一端是你基本上同步得很新的、近乎完美的代码库副本。它到底更靠近哪边？因为我觉得这种保真度我平时不太见得到。我猜它应该在中间某个位置。你讲讲看。

turns.en: It depends on the prototype. It's just a big directory of prototypes, and we have a component kit that’s close to Notion. It could be perfect if we spent more time on it, but we've tried to do the 80/20 thing — get it pretty close. We have a sidebar that looks kind of like Notion's sidebar, and buttons and dropdowns that are kind of like Notion's. Then it's up to each individual designer to push it as far as it needs to go to prove the point of their prototype. That's why I say it depends. For example, we have a designer here named Will Dawson. He's been working on the editor and the inline stuff you can do with AI while working on a Notion page. The only way to really feel what it's like to interact with AI while typing a page, selecting text, and navigating with your keyboard is to actually be in an editor. So in the prototype playground, he more or less recreated a simplified version of the Notion editor with slash commands and inline AI. The AI does real things — it writes back, updates the page in real time, selects stuff. It's very high fidelity; if you stare at it, you think, 'I think this is Notion.' But it's not. You have to push that far to really prove that the idea is good. Anyway, to answer your question, it's a wide range. We try to give some components to let people get close enough, but each designer can push as far as they want. Over time, I don't know what will happen. I think two things will happen. One is that we'll keep improving those components in the playground, so by default they look better and better. But I've also seen more and more designers skipping the playground and just iterating on designs directly in the production codebase. That's not appropriate for every type of work, but there’s an increasing number of things where it makes sense to just boot up the Notion codebase, throw Claude at the exact same problem, and you might as well get a real thing out the other side if you're going to spend roughly the same amount of time anyway.
turns.zh: 这取决于原型本身。它就是一个很大的原型目录，然后我们有一套组件库，跟 Notion 挺接近的。如果要投入更多时间，它也能做到完美，但我们一直想走 80/20 这条路——做到足够接近就行。我们有一个侧边栏，看起来有点像 Notion 的侧边栏；按钮和下拉框也跟 Notion 的差不多。然后每个设计师按自己的需要，把它推到他们想证明的那个点。这就是为什么我说要看情况。举个例子，我们这里有一位设计师叫 Will Dawson，他一直在做编辑器相关的功能，还有你在 Notion 页面上工作时可以和 AI 一起做的那些内联操作。要真正感受一边打字、一边选中文字、一边用键盘导航时和 AI 交互是什么感觉，唯一的办法就是真正进到编辑器里。所以在原型游乐场里，他差不多重新做了一个简化版的 Notion 编辑器，带了斜杠命令和内联 AI。这个 AI 会做真实的事情——真的写回、实时更新页面、选中内容。保真度非常高；你盯着它看的时候会觉得“这就是 Notion 吧”，但它并不是。你必须做到那种程度，才能真正证明这个想法是好的。总之，回到你的问题，它的范围很广。我们尽量提供一些组件让大家能快速接近目标，但每个设计师可以根据需要推到他们想要的任何程度。往后看，我不知道会发生什么。我觉得会有两件事发生：一是我们会继续改进游乐场里的组件，让它们默认情况下越来越好；二是我也看到越来越多的设计师根本跳过游乐场，直接在生产代码库里去迭代和设计。这并不适合所有类型的工作，但有越来越多的事情，与其花差不多同样的时间，不如直接启动 Notion 代码库，把 Claude 扔到同一个问题上，最后说不定你还能拿到一个真东西。

turns.en: How much of the Notion design team is actually touching production, working in code at all? Is it still acceptable to be doing mostly Figma work? Tell us.
turns.zh: Notion 的设计团队里，有多少人真的在碰生产环境、在写代码？现在还是以 Figma 工作为主也没什么问题吗？跟我们说说。

turns.en: I think it's totally fine, depending on what you're working on. But the barrier to entry for trying something in code is so low that I think everybody has dabbled with it.
turns.zh: 我觉得这完全没问题，取决于你在做什么。但用代码试一下的门槛实在是太低了，我觉得每个人都试过。

turns.en: What percentage of people go straight to production?
turns.zh: 有多大比例的人会直接去做生产环境的东西？

turns.en: I'm not sure. Maybe 10 to 20%, and it's still task-specific. There's still a lot of work that happens in Figma. A lot of people are playing with Paper now. I don't know — I feel like I'm surrounded by my people. We're all tinkering and trying the new things. But I think it's still about picking the right tool for the job. There are some types of design work where it's more helpful to be in a 2D canvas, taking screenshots and masking over them — 'Ah, I think this looks roughly right.' And then on the other side: 'No, I need the highest-fidelity version of this in a production environment.' We push the engineering team at Notion to make the codebase more legible to AI. A lot of the work that's happened under the hood — and I assume is happening at most companies — is around how to enable this type of work for people without engineering backgrounds, so the code they write with AI isn't terrible, doesn't break the service, is tested correctly, and gets reviewed correctly. A lot of that is codebase infrastructure stuff, from skill files to your actual CI pipeline, to make sure silly things don't slip through. As the company funnels more energy there, I feel like we'll all keep climbing this gradient toward trying things in production more often than not. But there will always be experimental, confusing ideas where it's better to sketch on a napkin or a whiteboard, or open Figma and draw some rectangles. Actually, these days a lot of people just open TLDraw and draw squares.
turns.zh: 我不确定。可能 10% 到 20%，而且这仍然是按任务分的。还是有很多工作在 Figma 里完成。也有很多人在玩 Paper。我不知道——我觉得身边都是我同类人，大家都在捣鼓、尝试新东西。但我觉得还是要为工作选对工具。有些设计工作，你就适合在 2D 画布里做，比如截图然后直接在图上蒙一层来改，心里想“嗯，这个看起来大致对了”。反过来，另一边就是想“不行，我需要在生产环境里拿到保真度最高的版本”。我们一直在推动 Notion 的工程团队，让代码库对 AI 更友好。所以很多幕后的工作——我相信大多数公司也在做——主要是怎么让没有工程背景的人也能这样工作，让他们用 AI 写的代码不至于很烂、不会搞挂服务、能正确测试、也能被正确评审。这很大程度上是代码库基础设施的活，从 skill 文件到真正的 CI 流水线，都是为了确保没有愚蠢的东西漏过去。随着公司往这个方向投入越来越多精力，我觉得我们都会沿着这个坡度往上走，越来越倾向于直接在生产环境里试。但总会有一些实验性的、模糊的想法，更适合在餐巾纸上画一画、在白板上写一写，或者打开 Figma 随便画几个方块。实际上，我觉得现在很多人会直接打开 TLDraw 画方块。

turns.en: As you move along that gradient, how does it change the way you collaborate and work together? What pieces of the design process that used to be staples have changed? How much does the medium change collaboration at Notion?
turns.zh: 随着你们沿着这个坡度往前走，协作和工作方式发生了什么样的变化？哪些以前是设计流程里标配的东西变了？媒介本身对 Notion 的协作方式影响有多大？

turns.en: I think it just moves from 'Hey, check out this Figma URL' to 'Hey, check out this deploy preview.' That's pretty much it. The artifact we're going to point at together and try together moves from one domain URL to another. That's been a big change. The prototype playground has been cool because it's all one codebase. You can poke around other people's stuff, yoink cool interactions from their prototypes, or duplicate theirs and riff on it. That type of interaction has been cool to see. But I don't know — we still have design crits. We show up in a meeting room, someone talks about the problem they're trying to solve, and maybe we share a different URL with each other.
turns.zh: 我觉得就是把“嘿，看看这个 Figma 链接”变成了“嘿，看看这个部署预览”。基本上就是这样。我们共同指向、共同试用的那个制品，它的域名从一个变成了另一个。这是一个很大的变化。原型游乐场之所以很酷，是因为它整个就在一个代码库里。你可以去翻别人做的东西，从别人的原型里偷点酷炫的交互，或者直接复制一份然后即兴发挥。这种互动方式很有意思。但我也说不好——我们还是有设计评审的。大家出现在会议室，某个人讲他们想解决的问题，然后我们可能互相分享一个不同的链接。

turns.en: It's kind of an in-the-weeds question, but when I think about what I thought my workflow would be like six months ago, looking into the future, I assumed I'd probably be doing a bunch of quick functional prototyping in code, and then really sweating the details on the canvas, fine-tuning all the visuals. And I found it's actually the complete opposite.
turns.zh: 这个问题有点细，但当我回想六个月前我以为自己的流程会是什么样子——就是那种展望未来的感觉——我以为我大概会做一大堆快速的代码功能原型，然后在画布上认真打磨细节、微调所有视觉效果。结果我发现，实际恰恰相反。

turns.en: Okay, 10,000 Wikipedia articles. How should we process that? A 10,000 Wikipedia article import happening simultaneously. Oh, I need to go learn about distributed systems and parallelization. What happens if one of those fails? Do we retry it? What happens if one of those Wikipedia articles is 30,000 words long and doesn't fit into a column of a database? So you get to hit all these little edge cases. And now what I'm having a lot of fun doing with Shuri is just going really deep handling all these edge cases, and at each step trying to write the test or the verification framework or add the logging necessary so that AI knows about all these edge cases and can design around them in the future.
turns.zh: 好，一万篇维基百科文章。我们应该怎么处理？同时导入一万篇维基百科文章。哦，我需要去学习分布式系统和并行化的知识。如果其中一篇失败了怎么办？要不要重试？如果其中一篇维基百科文章有三万词长，放不进数据库的一列里怎么办？所以你会碰到所有这些小边界情况。现在我玩 Shuri 玩得很开心的点，就是深入处理所有这些边界情况，并且每一步都尽量去写测试、验证框架，或者加上必要的日志，让 AI 知道所有这些边界情况，以后能绕开它们来设计。

turns.en: So this is very basic, but I'm kind of proud of this. The flow now is: when someone reports a bug on Shuri—and yes, bugs still happen—all I have to do is take their email address and paste it into Claude, or their user ID, whatever it is. I paste it into Claude. I have Claude hooked up to Sentry for error reporting and Supabase, so it can figure out information about their account. And I use Axiom as a log drain. I can just paste their user ID and the content of their email, and it will go and replay exactly what happened leading up to the moment of failure, because every single event is logged and tracked, all the exceptions and stuff. It knows what device they're on, all this kind of thing. So bug reporting and bug fixing has become quite fast.
turns.zh: 这很基本，但我有点自豪。现在的流程是：当有人在 Shuri 上报了一个 bug——没错，bug 还是会发生——我只需要把他们的邮箱地址粘贴到 Claude 里，或者用户 ID，随便什么。我把它粘贴进 Claude。我把 Claude 接上了 Sentry 做错误报告，还接了 Supabase，所以它能查到他们账户的信息。我用 Axiom 做日志收集。我只要粘贴他们的用户 ID 和邮件内容，它就会去重放失败前到底发生了什么，因为每一个事件都被记录和追踪，还有所有异常等等。它知道他们用什么设备，诸如此类。所以报告 bug 和修 bug 变得非常快。

turns.en: So to me, that is the fun part now. I feel like Shuri, you know the rock tumbler analogy from Steve Jobs? You put all these rough rocks in the thing and tumble them around. If you tumble it enough, what comes out is a set of polished stones. I'm having fun figuring out that part: what is the tumbler that lets me get a polished stone out the other side? Something that is resistant to edge cases, but if an edge case does come up, I'm able to find it very quickly and easily—or the AI finds it very quickly and easily on my behalf—and just fixes it and then adds that. So it's like a self-healing, self-reinforcing system. Not all of it's automated yet. In fact, very little of it is automated. But that's sort of the long-term goal: can I put more of this on rails, so that I can just focus on building cool and fun new features, and the infrastructure, the scaling, the edge case handling, the bugs—all that stuff is a self-healing loop.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，现在这才是好玩的部分。我觉得 Shuri，你知道史蒂夫·乔布斯那个岩石打磨机的比喻吗？你把所有粗粝的石头放进去，然后转动它。如果你转得够久，出来的就是一组抛光的石头。我现在就很享受搞清楚这部分：什么样的打磨机才能让我从另一头得到一个抛光的石头？一个能抵抗边界情况的东西，但万一出现边界情况，我也能非常快、非常容易地找到它——或者 AI 替我很快很容易地找到它——然后把它修好，再把这个情况加进去。所以这就像是一个自愈、自增强的系统。现在还不是全部自动化。事实上，自动化的部分很少。但这算是长期目标：我能不能把更多这种东西放到轨道上，让我可以专注于构建酷炫有趣的新功能，而基础设施、规模扩张、边界情况处理、bug——所有这些都变成一个自愈循环。

turns.en: The cool part for me about working with AI now is I get to stretch just beyond what I would have been comfortable doing as an engineer writing code before AI. I don't know. I want to build an API for Shuri. The 2024 version of me as a programmer would have been like, 'I don't really know where to even start. How would I build a CLI? How would I build an API? How would I do rate limiting? How would I do abuse detection? How would I do all these kinds of things?' And now all of a sudden, that type of work is very accessible. I can just guide the agent in that direction. That has been cool for Shuri. Like API, CLI, MCP—just pushing a little bit beyond my comfort zone. And I'm probably not pushing enough. As a designer who has been writing code for a while, it's hard to shake this mindset of 'oh, but how would I build this?' and get into this new way of working, which is: how would I describe my end vision or the end goal in a clear enough way that the AI can do it? It honestly made me go back to what you were talking about earlier, in terms of productivity and speed and everything. And I think I actually agree. It's weird. The dominant measuring stick that we use for AI is so often speed and efficiency. But I don't really care about that that much. That's not the impact it's had for me. It's not efficiency. It's like it's given me the ability to play in a set of adjacent ballparks that I previously had no business even walking into the door for. So it's more about raising the ceiling and increasing what I can bring to the table. I'm not necessarily doing that much stuff faster, but I'm doing many more different types of things that were previously inaccessible.
turns.zh: 现在和 AI 合作对我来说最酷的地方是，我可以伸展到以前作为一名写代码的工程师会觉得不舒服的领域。我不知道。我想给 Shuri 建一个 API。2024 年的我作为程序员可能会说：‘我真不知道从哪里开始。CLI 怎么建？API 怎么建？怎么做限流？怎么做滥用检测？怎么做这些所有东西？’而现在突然间，这类工作变得非常容易上手。我只要把智能体往那个方向引导就行。这对 Shuri 来说很酷。比如 API、CLI、MCP——就是稍微超出我的舒适区一点。而且我可能推得还不够。作为一个写了挺久代码的设计师，很难摆脱‘哦，但这个要怎么建？’的思维，进入这种新的工作方式，那就是：我该怎么清晰地描述我的最终愿景或最终目标，让 AI 能去实现它？这真的让我回到你之前说的那些，关于生产力和速度什么的。我想我其实同意。很奇怪。我们衡量 AI 的主要标准常常是速度和效率。但我不太在乎那个。那不是它对我的影响。不是效率。而是它让我能在一些邻近的领域里玩耍，那些领域我以前连门都进不去。所以这更像是抬高天花板，提升我能带来的东西。我不一定把很多事情做得更快，但我在做更多不同类型的事情，那些以前无法触及的事情。

turns.en: Shuri has kind of become a little bit of an antidote for me, because I spend my week at work like 'do more faster, write more code, build more prototypes.' And then I get to sit down with Shuri and think, 'What needs to be true for this to stay interesting and stay a project that I would work on for the next several years? What has to be true?' And part of that is I have to understand the codebase. I have to care about who's using it and that they're taken care of. I have to care about good infrastructure. And those things actually force you to slow down. I quite enjoy that. And what AI is allowing me to do is slow down and focus on the hard parts, and let the computer take care of the rest.
turns.zh: Shuri 对我来说有点像一剂解药，因为我上班时一周都在‘做更快、写更多代码、建更多原型’。然后我可以坐下来面对 Shuri 想：‘要让这个项目保持有趣、让我愿意接下来几年持续做下去，需要满足什么条件？什么必须是真实的？’其中一部分是我必须理解代码库。我必须关心谁在使用它，确保他们被照顾到。我必须关心好的基础设施。这些东西实际上逼你慢下来。我挺享受的。AI 让我能够做的是慢下来，专注在困难的部分，让电脑处理其余的事。

turns.en: So for example, my current workflow right now is: during the weeks I plan, and during the weekends I execute. So a typical day might be: I wake up, check and see if there are any errors overnight, or bugs, or user feedback. And then I just have a simple skill that's like 'fix issues,' and I can just paste that into Claude and let it go and fix all the Sentry issues or go debug things. Cool. That's off my plate. Now I can go talk to AI and like, 'I think I want to do this feature next, but I'm not quite sure how it's going to work. Here's roughly the intent or the user goal.' Submit. And then I go to work. And then I come back at night and I read the plan. And I'll chat with it for a little bit. And then maybe do one more round, submit, and then I go to bed. So that's one day. And then by Friday, Saturday morning, you've got a pretty good plan: 'Here's how I think I'm going to tackle this thing.' And then Saturday, all the nonsense is off my plate. There's not a pile of bugs to worry about. I just get to go and really study that plan and then get to work building it. I think that works for a side project. But I also like trying to be intentional about pacing myself. I scrambled a bit to get it out the door, as you have to do to get all the features in place. But now I want to get into a methodical rhythm: planning, shipping, polishing the stones, handling the edge cases. And just over time, maybe start slicing off little bits that can be automated. That's the interesting part.
turns.zh: 比如，我现在的日常流程是：工作日我计划，周末我执行。所以一个典型的日子可能是：我醒来，看看一夜之间有没有错误、bug 或用户反馈。然后我有一个简单技能叫‘修问题’，我可以直接把它粘贴进 Claude，让它去修所有 Sentry 的问题，或者去调试。酷，这不用我管了。然后我可以去跟 AI 说：‘我想下一步做这个功能，但我不太确定它会怎么运作。大概意图或用户目标是这样。’提交。然后我去工作。晚上回来我读计划。我会和它聊一会儿。然后可能再来一轮，提交，然后睡觉。所以这就是一天。然后到周五、周六早上，你会有一个相当好的计划：‘我觉得我会这样来搞这个东西。’然后周六，所有废话都不用我管。没有一堆 bug 要担心。我只需要去真正研究那个计划，然后开始构建。我觉得这对副业项目有用。但我也想要有意识地控制节奏。我有点赶着把它推出去，就像你必须把所有功能都就位一样。但现在我想进入一个有节奏的节拍：计划、发布、打磨石头、处理边界情况。然后随着时间推移，也许开始切出一些可以自动化的小块。那才是好玩的部分。

turns.en: Coming up on time here, I want to take a hard left, because there are a few potentially unrelated things that I honestly just kind of wanted to hear about. And one of them is, I'm hoping that you can heal some of my FOMO from Tokyo Design Conference, because you gave a talk there.
turns.zh: 时间快到了，我想来个急转弯，因为有几件可能不相关的事，我其实挺想听听。其中之一是，我希望你能治一治我对东京设计大会的错失恐惧症，因为你在那儿讲了话。

turns.en: And obviously we can't go do the whole thing, but when designers left that room after you were done, what was the core thing you were hoping they took away with them?
turns.zh: 显然我们没办法把整个演讲都讲一遍，但当你讲完之后，设计师们离开那个房间时，你希望他们带走的最核心的东西是什么？

turns.en: The thing I wanted people to take away from that talk is that AI is not magic. The underlying systems are very complicated. I don't think anybody would claim they know what an LLM's doing under the hood. But it is doing things on your computer like writing files, writing scripts, and invoking bash commands that were invented in the 70s. And those are knowable things. And there are two ways you can navigate that world. One is you can not pay attention to what AI is doing on your computer, the kind of code it's writing, how it writes the code, how it navigates your code base. You can just not pay attention and let the model take the wheel. Or you can be curious about it. Like, what does that mean? Wait, what is grep? And what's grep in relation to? Like sed? Sed, what's that? And you're going to find out about awk. And you're going to be like, what the—like some guy in the 70s just made this thing up, and it has stood the test of time. And now these three little commands are what power all modern agentic coding. It's insane. My manager at Notion, his name's Max Stoening. He's very, very good at nerd sniping me. And he nerd snipes me to be more curious about how computers work. He's sent me on a journey to play with Linux. He's sent me on a journey to understand what's happening when you boot up a terminal. And he's doing the same for many other people at Notion. Like, how do you demystify AI so that hopefully you can feel in control and wield it more effectively? Or just have a better opinion, or kind of see where the puck is going. Like, again, AI is using things that have been around for 50 years. And the people who know about these things are getting a lot of mileage. They're like, 'Oh, I know how computers work. I can point AI at this computer-shaped problem and get cool things out the other side.' So I think that's what I wanted people to take away from my talk. And the talk was really—I don't know—I shared some of the prompt examples I gave here, which is really about how do you just get the right upstream tokens that the AI can extrapolate from there. How can you nerd snipe yourself to understand what's happening when you hit submit on a prompt? I don't know if it was successful. But I hope at least one person became more curious after that.
turns.zh: 我希望大家从那个演讲中带走的一点是：AI 不是魔法。底层系统非常复杂。我不认为有谁敢说自己知道 LLM 在底层到底在做什么。但它的确在你的电脑上做一些事情，比如写文件、写脚本，或者调用 70 年代发明的 bash 命令。这些是可以认知的东西。面对这样一个世界，你有两种应对方式：一种是你完全不关注 AI 在你的电脑上做什么、它写的是什么样的代码、它怎么写代码、它如何浏览你的代码库；你可以完全放手，让模型接管方向盘。另一种是你可以对它感到好奇。比如，那是什么意思？等等，grep 是什么？grep 和什么相关？比如 sed？sed 又是啥？然后你会去了解 awk。你可能会想：天哪，70 年代某个家伙发明了这个东西，居然一直经久不衰。而如今，就是这三个小命令支撑起了所有现代的智能体式编码。这太疯狂了。我在 Notion 的经理叫 Max Stoening，他特别擅长对我进行技术勾引。他勾引我对计算机的工作原理产生更多好奇。他让我去玩 Linux，让我去理解打开终端时发生了什么。他也在对 Notion 的很多其他人做同样的事。比如，如何破除 AI 的神秘感，让你能更好地掌控它、更有效地使用它？或者只是让你有一个更好的判断，或者看到大势所趋。再说一次，AI 正在使用那些已经存在了 50 年的东西。而了解这些东西的人正在获得巨大的收益。他们会觉得，哦，我了解计算机的工作原理，我可以把 AI 指向一个计算机形状的问题，然后从另一端得到很酷的东西。所以这就是我希望人们从我的演讲中带走的。这个演讲其实……怎么说呢，我分享了一些我在这里给出的 prompt 示例，这其实关乎如何拿到正确的上游 token，让 AI 能够从中进行外推。你怎么能让自己去好奇、去理解点击提交 prompt 的那一刻发生了什么。我不知道是否成功，但我希望至少有一件事让人变得更加好奇。

turns.en: The comment about Max and nerd sniping makes me want to go down another little rabbit hole, because Max is someone I guess I've always looked up to from a distance. I've never met Max, never worked with him. And I think it is representative of almost the way I view Notion as a whole. There's obviously a bunch of really talented people there building really incredible software. I've never really been in any environment like that before. So you're now over a year in. How do you think either that culture, or the people, or the way of working—how else has that shaped you as a designer over the last year plus?
turns.zh: 你提到 Max 和技术勾引，这让我想再深挖一下另一个小问题，因为 Max 是我一直以来远远仰视的人。我从未见过 Max，也没有和他共事过。我觉得这几乎代表了我看待 Notion 这个整体的方式。那里显然有一群非常有才华的人在构建非常了不起的软件。我从来没有真正待在过那样的环境里。所以你现在已经入职一年多了。你觉得那种文化、那些人，或者那种工作方式——还有哪些方面塑造了你过去这一年多作为设计师的自己？

turns.en: The cool part about Notion right now is that, from top to bottom, we are very comfortable revisiting old assumptions. Does Notion really need to look like this? Will it be this shape forever? And we're starting to poke and prod at that. Some of the designers on the team just redid the left sidebar, making it much more of a chat-forward experience. A lot of us internally have pretty much used Notion through chat or through agents. The willingness to embrace that, to change, and to question all the assumptions is very cool. I think that is a hard thing for a company at this size to do, because it's scary, right? Things are going well, but the world's going to look very different in a few years, and we need to be ready for it. And then I think the second part of that, and what Max is good at and what the leadership here is good at doing, is encouraging people to think bigger. I think right now OpenAI and Anthropic are way more YOLO about, like, 'Wouldn't it be crazy if we did this?' And I think there are a lot of software companies that are a little bit scared to ask that of themselves. It feels outside their cultural permission boundary—the permission to play in that space. And so, yeah, I think Max and everyone else is good at pushing people to ask, 'Why not?' Like, 'Why can't we?' Here's Notion's box, right? People think of Notion as a wiki, a note-taking tool, a document collaboration tool. What's right outside that box that's really interesting? Let's go play there. And that is a very fun place to be. Yeah, we're like two days from Linear or Karai publishing the article saying issue tracking is dead. And I'm like, how many companies on the planet would do that type of thing? I do think Notion is potentially one of them. But it's such a weird moment in SaaS. Like you said, everything on paper could be going well, but if you're not looking however many years ahead—if there's one thing that's certain, it's that the amount of change in two years is going to be extraordinary. Nobody knows for certain, but it seems like a good idea for every company right now to understand how to make your systems legible to AI, so that you can participate in that ecosystem in the future. Seems like the ecosystem won't go away. We don't know exactly what the agents will be doing or how they'll want to work in the future, so you just need to design your software in a somewhat flexible way. Which is why we come back to things like APIs and CLIs. These things have existed for a long time. Computers know how to use them. They're not going to go away for a long time. So let's invest in those things, right? I think we just shipped a Notion CLI. Notion's not historically a developer tool. We have a developer platform where you can build integrations and build stuff for your team. But hey, Notion has a CLI, so that everything you can do through the Notion API is now legible to an AI. And of course we were very early with MCP and all that kind of stuff. These are the things I think you have to be doing to poke at the edges and make sure you're in a good position to move quickly as the models change shape or new capabilities come out. So, yeah, kudos to Karai and the Linear team, and to any company that is doing that—really taking an honest look at their current business in this new world we're living in. If they're not doing that, they're in trouble, I think.
turns.zh: 现在 Notion 最酷的一点是，从上到下我们都非常愿意重新审视旧的假设。Notion 真的需要长这样吗？它会永远是这个形状吗？我们开始去戳一戳、捅一捅这些问题。比如，团队里的一些设计师刚刚重做了左侧边栏，让它的体验更像聊天。我们内部很多人基本上都是通过聊天或者智能体来使用 Notion。这种愿意接纳变化、质疑所有假设的态度非常棒。我觉得对于这个规模的公司来说，能做到这一点很难，因为这很吓人，对吧？现在一切进展顺利，但几年后世界会大不一样，我们必须为此做好准备。然后是第二点，Max 擅长的、这里的领导层擅长的，就是鼓励大家想得更大。我觉得现在的 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 要‘管他呢’得多，会想‘如果我们这么做会不会很疯狂？’而我觉得很多软件公司都不太敢这样问自己。这感觉超出了他们的文化许可边界——允许自己在那片空间里玩的边界。所以，是的，我觉得 Max 和其他人都在推动大家问‘为什么不呢？’比如，‘我们为什么不能？’这里是 Notion 的盒子，对吧？人们把 Notion 想象成一个维基、一个笔记工具、一个文档协作工具。那盒子外面有什么真正有趣的东西？我们去那里玩吧。那是一个非常好玩的地方。是的，我们离 Linear 或 Karai 发表文章说‘问题追踪已死’大概也就两天。我就想说，这个世界上有多少公司会做那种事？我确实认为 Notion 有可能是其中之一。但这是 SaaS 领域一个非常奇怪的时刻。就像你所说，纸面上一切可能都好，但如果你不看几年之后——如果有一件事是确定的，那就是两年内的变化幅度将是惊人的。没有人能百分百确定，但对每家公司来说，现在似乎都应该理解如何让你的系统对 AI 可读，以便你未来能参与那个生态。看起来这个生态不会消失。我们不知道智能体到底会做什么，也不知道它们未来想以什么方式工作，所以你只需要把你的软件设计得有一定灵活性。这也是为什么我们会回到 API 和 CLI。这些东西已经存在很久了。计算机知道怎么用它们。它们在很长一段时间内都不会消失。所以，让我们投资这些东西吧，对吧？我觉得我们刚刚发布了 Notion CLI。Notion 历来不是一个开发者工具。我们有一个开发者平台，你可以构建集成，为你的团队构建东西。但嘿，Notion 有了 CLI，这样你通过 Notion API 能做的一切现在都对 AI 可读了。当然，我们很早就开始做 MCP 之类的东西。我认为你必须做这些事情来探索边界，确保自己处于一个能快速行动的有利位置，以应对模型形态变化或新能力的出现。所以，是的，也要给 Karai 和 Linear 团队点赞，以及任何正在这样做的公司——真正诚实地看待自己在当下这个世界中的业务。如果他们没有这样做，我觉得他们会有麻烦。

turns.en: Final question. Maybe we could shift from company strategy to personal, more career strategy for a second, because—oh boy.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。也许我们可以暂时把话题从公司战略转到个人职业战略，因为——哦，天哪。
